newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Aboriginal boys held for spitting at Australian MP.
newsitem.headline: Aboriginal boys held for spitting at Australian MP.

text.p: Aboriginal groups reacted angrily on Saturday to news that two young Aboriginal boys were being held without bail in conservative Queensland state for spitting at controversial Australian politician Pauline Hanson.

Media reports said four Aborigines aged between nine and 12 visited Hanson in her Queensland constituency office on Wednesday, first claiming to be supporters but then spitting at the independent conservative parliamentarian.
One of them was too young to be arrested, but three others appeared in a local court on Thursday and two brothers, aged 11 and 12, were remanded without bail until January 30. The fourth was bailed.

Hanson, a blunt-speaking owner of a fish and chip shop, has driven an emotional debate on race and immigration since complaining in her maiden parliamentary speech in September that Aborigines were being given unfair government aid and the country risked being swamped by Asians.
Her remarks struck a chord with Australian voters and embarrassed mainstream political parties. The race row has also seen a rise in anti-Asian feeling and incidents of abuse against non-whites.

An Ipswich police officer, who did not want to be named, said the three boys had been charged with aggravated assault and unlawful assembly. One had also been charged with wilful damage to police property.
The officer added that the boys might appeal against the bail ruling in the Queensland Supreme Court in Brisbane on Monday.
Hanson told Australian television that she supported the court's ruling. "People have to be made responsible for their actions and I don't care how old they are," she said.

But the decision to remand the boys was heavily criticised by the Aboriginal Deaths in Custody Watch Committee, which campaigns against the disproportionate number of indigenous Australians being held in the country's jails.

"People are absolutely horrified by this," Committee spokesman Ray Jackson told Reuters. "We're not condoning that kids come off the street and do this but you have to look at the reasons behind it -- Hanson's bad vibes have built up such a lot of bad feeling, especially in Ipswich.
"When people are spitting at Asians, there seems to be very little action by the police on those occasions."

The incident will come as an embarrassment to the Queensland state government, which has announced plans to spend an extra A$1 million (US$790,000) to attract foreign tourists to its tropical beaches after a successful visit by U.S. President Bill Clinton in to the Great Barrier Reef in November.

A report last week said that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children were more than 20 times as likely to be held in juvenile detention centres than non-indigenous children. In Queensland they were 41 times more likely to be detained.
Jackson said 110 Aborigines had died in custody nationwide since May 1989 and at least six had died in Queensland prisons this year.
